absent: Exact binary layout, sizes, and offsets of task, floating point, saved-state, header, and shadow-stack structures beyond names seen.
Semantics of permission inheritance, dynamic feature handling, shadow-stack update, trace points, and protection-key management.
Lock ordering, sleepability, scheduler interaction, and interrupt rules beyond the local warnings shown.
Trap entry, signal delivery, return paths, and fault-table mechanics that consume the codes and hooks.
Full extended-state feature enumeration, supervisor versus user partition, and hardware restore semantics.
Debugger core, bounded-buffer mechanics, allocation failure paths, and emulation fallbacks not routed here.

findings.text: Clone preparation establishes a fresh floating point context for a new task, marking it absent from hardware, resetting its software state, requesting a reload before user execution, and either installing a minimal initial image or inheriting the current user image under protection, with permission inheritance only for non-thread clones, clearing of device address state, and shadow stack synchronization that can request special handling.

The floating point context resides immediately after the task descriptor with cacheline alignment enforced at build time, starts life marked as residing on no processor, and its register image offset and size for hardened copying are derived from the task and register layout combined with the configured default state size.

A per-task need-load marker tracks whether hardware holds current user registers. Clearing operations, supervisor synchronization, reloads from the initial image, activation marking, and consistency checks move between loaded and need-load states, while drop and flush paths reset the association without altering stored hardware values until next user entry.

Register save, restore, validation and activation sequences execute under the floating point register lock, drop additionally disables preemption around the current-task deactivation, and the lock-and-load helper warns when invoked in a context where floating point use in interrupts is unsafe or from a kernel thread.

Thread flush, return-to-user, and idle hooks provide lifecycle entry points: one resets software state and register image for the current thread, one ensures user registers are present when floating point support exists, and one releases tile resources and clears ownership when tile features are active during idle.

Exception classification distinguishes legacy x87 faults from SIMD faults, combining control and status information to select invalid-operation, divide-by-zero, overflow, underflow-or-denormal, or precision signal codes, returning zero when no recognized unmasked condition is present to allow for spurious traps.

State is viewed through overlapping legacy, extended-save, and 512-bit media layouts with a header tracking present features, a supervisor portion restored separately, a protection-key field carried alongside the task, and a shadow-stack component located by feature identifier; user images are copied through a bounded buffer abstraction.

Supervisor-only restoration derives a supervisor feature mask and applies it in low and high halves to the extended-save area, used to bring supervisor components into registers before user state handling.

Legacy save and restore helpers isolate faults: user-frame accesses permit page faults and report failure safely with access-hardening toggles, while kernel accesses capture errors via exception tables; 32-bit and 64-bit forms select the appropriate mnemonic width.
Availability probes for debug register sets report full width when the relevant extension or shadow-stack feature is enabled for the target, otherwise zero, gating subsequent get and set operations.

Debugger access synchronizes only when the target is the current task, and any external modification first invalidates the hardware association so later use reloads from memory; modification of the running task through this path is treated as a programming error.

Extended and media register-set access requires exact whole-buffer transfers, validates the media control value against allowed feature bits, clears upper vector slots for 32-bit callers, marks corresponding presence bits on write, and stages user buffers dynamically when no kernel copy is supplied.

Shadow-stack pointer access exposes a single aligned value below the user address limit, requires the shadow-stack extension and per-task enablement, synchronizes state before reading, and invalidates hardware association before updating the stored pointer.

Tag-word translation preserves stack occupancy across formats: one direction compresses two-bit tags into empty-or-valid bits packed into a byte, the other reconstructs empty, zero, valid, or special classifications from occupancy, stack top, exponent range, and significand content with address computation for rotated slots.

Legacy 32-bit environment translation exchanges control, status, tag, instruction and data pointers, and eight register slots between compact and extended forms, sourcing code segment and data segment differently on 64-bit kernels versus 32-bit kernels, and debug get and set paths select among software emulation, legacy, and extended sources with presence-bit maintenance.
The media control feature mask starts with all 32 bits set and is fixed after initialization, defining the set of values accepted on writes to the media control field.
Legacy tag classifications encode valid as zero, zero as one, special as two, and empty as three, and the internal and legacy headers each establish a single inclusion guard.
